title: Kerala CM Deadlock: Congress Still Can't Pick a Winner
excerpt: A marathon Delhi summit between Kharge, Rahul Gandhi and three rival contenders ends without a decision, exposing deep factional fault lines.
body:
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge hosted a high-stakes, three-hour summit at his New Delhi residence on Saturday, May 9 — and Kerala still does not have a chief minister. The party's historic win of 102 seats in the 140-member assembly has given way to an embarrassingly public leadership battle that shows no sign of ending.

**What happened in Delhi:**
Rahul Gandhi sat across from all three contenders — outgoing Leader of Opposition V.D. Satheesan, AICC General Secretary K.C. Venugopal, and veteran leader Ramesh Chennithala — alongside KPCC president Sunny Joseph and AICC observers Mukul Wasnik and Ajay Maken. After hours of deliberation, AICC observer Deepa Dasmunsi confirmed the final decision had been deferred entirely to the party high command, with no announcement imminent. All three leaders then made a rare joint public appeal, urging supporters to pull down the 'poster war' raging across Kerala — and by Saturday night, Youth Congress workers were removing flex boards from party offices in Thiruvananthapuram and beyond.

**Why this is more than just jostling:**
Venugopal, widely seen as Rahul Gandhi's closest organisational ally, reportedly holds the backing of over 40 Congress MLAs. Satheesan, however, commands the street — credited with engineering the UDF's sweep of 18 of 20 Lok Sabha seats in 2024 and leading the campaign against Pinarayi Vijayan's decade-long LDF government. The Indian Union Muslim League, the UDF's most powerful ally with 22 seats, has signalled preference for Satheesan. Chennithala stakes his claim on seniority alone. Analysts warn that whoever loses could refuse cabinet entry or even trigger a costly bypoll, echoing the bruising Karnataka succession fight of 2023 between Siddaramaiah and D.K. Shivakumar.

**What to watch:**
With the new Kerala Assembly constitutionally required to be formed before May 23, the Congress high command faces a hard clock — and its next move will test whether Rahul Gandhi can impose discipline on a party still defined by its factions.
